title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 53–54
description: Advanced medical-language vocabulary, clinical versus informal wording, medical metaphors, nutrition and physical-fitness expressions, and metaphors from sport.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied Advanced textbook. Vocabulary targets were checked against teaching pages and relevant exercises and the answer key. All translations, usage notes and teaching examples were written anew; original exercises, diagrams and longer textbook passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Complete teaching and exercise pages for Units 53–54, including medical information leaflet vocabulary, figurative medical language, nutrition and fitness topics, sport metaphors, footnotes, and exercise/answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA only for targets with sufficiently confident phonemic forms; longer phrases and uncertain cases are left blank. Browser-specific connected speech and accent variants are not claimed to have been verified.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing content and audit metadata are written in English, except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared PDF teaching text, figures, exercises and answer key. Checked words against unit purposes, medical and figurative senses, register, British usage, translation, IPA, original examples and provenance; ran local schema, IDs and static audio-target checks.
audit.limitations: No recorded MP3s are bundled. Actual VocabLab browser import, speech synthesis and recognition remain untested. Medical terminology is included for language study, not diagnosis or treatment advice. Nutrition and BMI statements in the source are not independently validated as clinical guidance.

units.title: Unit 53 — Medical language
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 112–113 (PDF pages 114–115).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Health and medicine · information leaflets and metaphorical medical language
learningObjectives: Interpret the specialist wording of medicine leaflets, including dosage, medical history, adverse reactions and bodily symptoms.
Distinguish clinical and colloquial alternatives such as stools, excrement and poo, and feel sick from be sick.
Use medical metaphors precisely in writing about social and organisational problems.
Recognise figurative changes of meaning in prognosis, ailing, fever pitch, jaundiced and contagious.

sectionsChecked: All teaching text and definitions in sections A and B
Figures, footnotes, word-use contrasts and all exercise questions
Exercise answers and related vocabulary explanations in the answer key

items.pt: bula informativa; folheto de informações médicas
items.example: The pharmacist handed her a medical information leaflet with the medicine.
items.note: A patient-facing document explaining precautions, use and possible unwanted effects.

items.example: The leaflet advised readers to report whether they were taking low-dose aspirin.
items.note: Low-dose specifies a small prescribed amount rather than a standard pain-relief dose; this is a vocabulary example, not treatment advice.

items.example: The dosage table gave the dose prescribed for each age group.
items.note: An individual measured amount of a medicine; distinct from the duration of treatment.

items.example: The study examined how people with asthma understood medication labels.
items.note: Respiratory condition; adjective asthmatic.

items.example: The new doctor reviewed the patient's medical history before the consultation.
items.note: The record of previous conditions and treatments; not medical story.

items.pt: ter histórico de; apresentar antecedentes de
items.example: The form asked whether any family members had a history of heart disease.
items.note: Pattern: have a history of an illness or condition.

items.pt: doença do tecido conjuntivo; distúrbio do tecido conjuntivo
items.example: The specialist explained what the term connective tissue disorder meant on the referral.
items.note: Technical label for a condition affecting tissues that support or connect body structures.

items.pt: doença gastrointestinal; doença do trato digestivo
items.example: The report grouped several stomach and intestinal conditions under gastrointestinal disease.
items.note: Gastrointestinal relates to the stomach and intestines, not all medical conditions.

items.example: The clinician used the word bowel when explaining the digestive system.
items.note: A medical and everyday term for the intestine; often appears in bowel problems.

items.example: The researchers recorded every suspected adverse reaction during the trial.
items.note: A harmful or unwanted response, often to a medicine; more formal and specific than feeling unwell.

items.example: The medical glossary described a stroke as an interruption of blood supply to part of the brain.
items.note: The cardiovascular meaning in the unit, not a swimming stroke or a brushstroke.

items.example: The form asked participants to list any long-term medical condition.
items.note: A broad term for an illness, disorder or other health problem.

items.pt: correr risco de; estar sujeito a
items.example: The brochure explained which groups might be at risk of complications.
items.note: Pattern: be at risk of something; not simply at risk to something.

items.example: The warning clearly said not to exceed the stated dose.
items.note: Exceed means go beyond a specified limit; dose is an amount, not a time period.

items.example: The trial compared the duration of treatment across the groups.
items.note: Duration means the length of time something continues.

items.example: The package insert listed dizziness as a possible side effect.
items.note: An unintended effect alongside the intended effect; not all side effects are necessarily severe.

items.example: The clinician asked about any previous allergic reaction to medication.
items.note: Response associated with an allergy; different from a general adverse reaction.

items.example: She described the feeling as nausea rather than pain.
items.note: Formal noun for the sensation of wanting to vomit; adjective nauseous.

items.example: The instruction leaflet used vomit as a formal alternative to be sick.
items.note: A verb or noun for bringing up stomach contents; in British English be sick can have the same meaning.

items.example: He had been sick during the night and was still feeling weak.
items.note: In British English be sick often means vomit, whereas feel sick commonly means nauseated.

items.example: The leaflet directed readers to seek medical help if serious symptoms developed.
items.note: Formal instruction meaning obtain assistance from a healthcare professional.

items.example: The laboratory examined tiny particles in the sample.
items.note: A small piece of matter; plural particles appears in the medical leaflet.

items.example: The clinician explained why the laboratory might request a sample of stools.
items.note: Standard medical term for faeces in this context; usually plural.

items.example: The scientific article used excrement rather than a more conversational term.
items.note: Formal term for bodily waste; contrasts with informal poo.

items.pt: cocô; fezes, em linguagem infantil ou informal
items.example: The parent used the word poo while speaking to the toddler.
items.note: Informal, often child-directed British English, rather than clinical wording.

items.example: The case report mentioned temporary disorientation after the incident.
items.note: State of being confused about place, time or circumstances.

items.pt: sintoma de um problema mais profundo; indício de problema estrutural
items.example: The repeated delays may be a symptom of a deeper problem with project planning.
items.note: Figurative symptom points to an underlying issue rather than a disease.

items.example: Changing the schedule would not solve the underlying problem.
items.note: Underlying suggests an important cause that is not immediately visible.

items.example: The confusion was symptomatic of poor communication between departments.
items.note: Formal pattern: something is symptomatic of a broader issue.

items.pt: diagnosticar um problema; identificar suas causas
items.example: The consultants were hired to diagnose the problems affecting the organisation.
items.note: A medical verb extended to identifying causes of social, economic or technical difficulties.

items.example: The analyst offered a cautious prognosis for the peace negotiations.
items.note: A medical prediction of how illness will develop, used figuratively for likely outcomes.

items.example: The new director was asked to revive the ailing company.
items.note: Literally unwell; figuratively struggling or in decline.

items.pt: uma onda de; uma série repentina de
items.example: A rash of complaints prompted the hotel to review its booking system.
items.note: Here rash means a sudden cluster of similar events, not a skin eruption.

items.example: Speculation reached fever pitch before the final decision.
items.note: Figurative extreme excitement or intensity; commonly reach fever pitch.

items.pt: atingir o auge da tensão ou excitação
items.example: Interest in the election reached fever pitch during the televised debate.
items.note: Fixed collocation for intensity climbing to a peak.

items.pt: visão cética e negativa de; olhar desconfiado sobre
items.example: Years of failed promises had left her with a jaundiced view of the industry.
items.note: Figurative scepticism often shaped by disappointing experiences; jaundiced also has a clinical meaning.

items.pt: carregar as marcas de; ter sequelas emocionais de
items.example: The community still carries the scars of the prolonged dispute.
items.note: Metaphorical lasting harm from a difficult experience; scars are physical marks literally.

items.example: Several former employees said they had been scarred by the toxic working culture.
items.note: Passive pattern referring to lasting emotional or social damage.

items.example: Her determination seemed to infect others with enthusiasm for the project.
items.note: Figurative passing on of an attitude; not a claim about transmitting an illness.

items.word: have your finger on the pulse
items.pt: estar por dentro do que está acontecendo; acompanhar as tendências
items.example: The editor has her finger on the pulse of changing reader preferences.
items.note: Means understand current developments or public attitudes; often with of.

items.pt: uma onda de; sequência concentrada de
items.example: The city recorded a spate of complaints about late-night noise.
items.note: A number of similar undesirable incidents in a short period.

items.pt: paralisado; impedido de funcionar ou agir
items.example: The unexpected shutdown left the entire transport network paralysed.
items.note: Metaphorical inability to function; physically paralysed describes loss of movement.

items.pt: fatal; desastroso; decisivo para o fracasso
items.example: A fatal flaw in the proposal led to its rejection.
items.note: Figuratively disastrous or ruinous, not necessarily causing a death.

items.example: Her optimism was contagious and lifted the mood of the team.
items.note: Metaphorically something that spreads between people, such as an attitude or enthusiasm.

items.pt: doença; mal social, em sentido figurado
items.example: The columnist described corruption as a disease affecting several institutions.
items.note: In metaphorical language, disease represents a persistent harmful problem.

units.title: Unit 54 — Diet, sport and fitness
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 114–115 (PDF pages 116–117).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Health and fitness · nutrition, physical activity and sporting metaphors
learningObjectives: Use natural collocations for diet and heart-related terminology, including cholesterol-rich foods and high-fibre diets.
Discuss physical activity with vocabulary for calories, metabolism, body mass index, and brisk walking.
Use idiomatic metaphors from football, horse racing, skating and sailing with correct constructions.
Distinguish the textbook’s vocabulary focus from personalised or scientifically established medical advice.

sectionsChecked: All teaching text and definitions in sections A, B and C
Figures, footnotes, word-use contrasts and all exercise questions
Exercise answers and related vocabulary explanations in the answer key

items.example: The diagram showed an artery carrying blood away from the heart.
items.note: An artery normally carries blood away from the heart; contrast vein.

items.example: The researchers investigated how the treatment affected blood flow.
items.note: Flow refers to the movement of blood through vessels.

items.example: The narrow passage impeded the movement of the equipment.
items.note: Formal verb meaning obstruct or slow progress; used medically of blood flow.

items.example: The textbook diagram showed fatty plaque inside an artery.
items.note: In this context, a build-up of material along the arterial wall.

items.example: Grease can clog a narrow drain if it builds up over time.
items.note: Verb meaning block a passage; the source uses it for arteries.

items.example: The laboratory report included a measurement of cholesterol.
items.note: A fat-like substance found in the body; blood tests distinguish several lipid measures.

items.example: The article discussed cholesterol-rich foods and dietary choices.
items.note: Compound adjective; attaches to food or other nouns without implying a simple rule about health.

items.example: The chef planned nutritious meals using vegetables and pulses.
items.note: Means supplying nutrients the body needs; noun nutrition.

items.example: The course included a module on nutrition and public health.
items.note: Noun connected with nutritious; not a synonym for dieting.

items.example: The report suggested that treats could still be enjoyed in moderation.
items.note: A fixed phrase meaning without excess; common in discussions of food and alcohol.

items.pt: representar um perigo; constituir um risco
items.example: Faulty wiring could pose a danger to people using the laboratory.
items.note: Collocation: pose a danger or risk to someone or something.

items.example: The nutrition label gave the amount of fibre in each serving.
items.note: British spelling; American English fiber.

items.example: The pamphlet explained what a high-fibre diet might include.
items.note: High-fibre is a compound adjective; common in nutrition guidance.

items.example: The article listed lentils among several fibre-rich foods.
items.note: Adjective -rich follows the nutrient name; British spelling fibre.

items.example: The recipe combined lentils with tomatoes and herbs.
items.note: A pulse, commonly used in dishes containing dietary fibre and protein.

items.pt: aveia em flocos ou farinha de aveia, conforme o uso
items.example: The breakfast menu offered oatmeal with sliced fruit.
items.note: May mean ground oats or an oat-based breakfast dish, depending on region.

items.example: She bought wholemeal bread for the sandwiches.
items.note: British term for bread made with wholegrain flour; American whole-wheat bread.

items.example: The presentation showed how blood vessels connect organs and tissues.
items.note: General term covering arteries, veins and capillaries.

items.example: The public information campaign explained how a heart attack differs from a stroke.
items.note: A heart event involving interrupted blood supply to heart muscle; distinct from stroke.

items.example: The lesson contrasted a stroke with a heart attack.
items.note: Here stroke concerns disrupted blood supply in the brain; not interchangeable with heart attack.

items.example: The study compared different kinds of cardiovascular exercise.
items.note: Activity involving the heart and circulation; cardiovascular is an adjective.

items.example: The leaflet used the term diabetic when discussing insulin-related vocabulary.
items.note: Used as noun or adjective, though person with diabetes is common in person-first medical communication.

items.example: The diagram explained the role of insulin in glucose regulation.
items.note: A hormone involved in regulating blood glucose; not a generic energy supplement.

items.example: Cycling to work can be one way to burn calories through activity.
items.note: Everyday expression for expending energy; burn is figurative rather than literal combustion.

items.pt: esportivo; que gosta ou pratica esportes
items.example: You do not need to be particularly sporty to enjoy an evening walk.
items.note: Informal adjective describing someone interested in or good at sport.

items.example: The biology lecture introduced the concept of metabolism.
items.note: Processes through which the body uses and transforms energy and substances.

items.example: The article discussed the phrase speed up your metabolism and what it means.
items.note: Common fitness wording; it should not be taken as a guaranteed consequence of any particular workout.

items.example: The researchers recorded body mass index alongside several other measurements.
items.note: BMI is calculated from height and weight; it is not a direct measurement of body fat.

items.example: The form asked for height and weight so the system could calculate BMI.
items.note: Initialism for body mass index, normally spoken as three separate letters in English.

items.pt: estar determinado a; estar decidido a
items.example: She was intent on improving her running technique before the next race.
items.note: Pattern: be intent on + noun or -ing form, not to + infinitive here.

items.pt: caminhada rápida; caminhada em ritmo acelerado
items.example: The timetable included a short session of brisk walking each morning.
items.note: Brisk means quick and energetic; used especially with walking.

items.example: He took up jogging to spend more time outdoors.
items.note: Gentler running rather than a formal competitive sport.

items.example: The team monitored whether the programme could lower blood pressure.
items.note: Verb + noun collocation; it describes an effect to be measured, not an assured outcome.

items.pt: dar um tiro no próprio pé; prejudicar os próprios interesses
items.example: By insulting the panel, the candidate scored an own goal during the interview.
items.note: From football: do something intended to help but which actually damages your position.

items.pt: mudar as regras no meio do jogo; alterar critérios inesperadamente
items.example: The client kept moving the goalposts after the contract had been signed.
items.note: From football; often implies an unfair or frustrating change in requirements.

items.pt: condições justas e iguais de competição
items.example: The regulator wanted a level playing field for small and large suppliers.
items.note: From sport; a fair situation in which participants face comparable conditions.

items.pt: estar na disputa por; ter chance real de conquistar
items.example: She is in the running for the new research fellowship.
items.note: From racing; be seriously considered for an award, job or opportunity.

items.pt: empatados; lado a lado em uma disputa
items.example: The two proposals were neck and neck in the final evaluation.
items.note: From horse racing; competitors have almost the same chance of winning.

items.pt: fugir da questão; evitar tratar diretamente do assunto
items.example: The spokesperson repeatedly skated around the issue of funding.
items.note: From skating; avoid addressing a difficult subject directly.

items.pt: passar facilmente por; superar sem dificuldade
items.example: Despite the demanding selection process, she sailed through the interviews.
items.note: From sailing; complete a task, examination or process with apparent ease.

items.example: The recipe collection highlighted several protein-rich vegetarian dishes.
items.note: -rich combines with a nutrient to mean containing a comparatively large amount of it.

items.example: The menu described the vegetable dish as vitamin-rich.
items.note: Same compound pattern as fibre-rich, with rich following the nutrient.
